scribe_response.text: Tell me about a teacher or a mentor who influenced you. The teacher who influenced me most was Missus Ledesma, the principal of my first school. She was tall and thin, with silver hair, and wore the same gray dress every Monday. When I arrived at twenty-two, I was full of ideas and short on experience. My first morning I wrote a long lesson plan on the board, and thirty children stared. By ten o'clock half of them were asleep, and the others were drawing on their arms. Missus Ledesma had stood at the back, and she waited until um the bell rang. Then she asked me gently whether I had looked at the children or only at my plan. I was um ashamed, but I knew she was right, because I had been um teaching to the um wall. She invited me to her office, a tiny room with a battered desk and a pot of orchids. She poured me hot calamansi juice and told me about her own terrible first day. She had once been so nervous uh that she fainted into a, a bucket of chalk. We laughed until we cried, and from then on I could ask her anything. Over the next years she taught me um to teach with my eyes, my hands, and my whole face. What happened next? She said a child can forgive a teacher almost anything except um boredom, boredom. She showed me how to turn a lesson about fractions into a story about sharing a cake. We cut paper plates, and the children learned that half is uh not a quarter. Once she brought a live crab to class so we could study how uh it walked sideways. It escaped, and chaos followed, but I um never forgot what a claw looks like. She believed in noticing the quiet children, the ones who sat by the window. She kept a little notebook and wrote one good thing about each child every week. I copied that habit, and I have filled many notebooks over the decades. When a boy named Ernesto could not read, she did not uh scold him or send him away. She stayed after school with him for months, using flashcards made from cereal boxes. By the end of the year Ernesto read aloud at the um assembly, and half the audience wept. I watched all this and learned that patience is the real engine of teaching. Missus Ledesma was also strict about punctuality, tidy shelves, and polished shoes. She said order gives children a sense of safety, and safety lets them be brave. Can you tell me more about that? She never raised, raised her voice, and her silence was more powerful than any shouting. When I told her I planned to move abroad, she was quiet for a long time. Then she uh took one orchid from the pot and said it should travel with me. She wrapped um it in damp newspaper, and I carried it in my handbag on the airplane. It survived the flight and bloomed in my first apartment, a small purple miracle. Missus Ledesma passed away a few years later, and I could not attend her funeral. I lit a candle in my church in Abu Dhabi and sang her favorite hymn in the kitchen. Many of the orchids on my balcony today are great grandchildren of that um first plant. Whenever a new bloom opens, I think of her gray dress and calm voice. When I trained young teachers, I told them the story of the crab and the notebook. Teaching is not about the plan on the board but about the faces in the room. I hope that somewhere a child remembers me the way I remember her. A good mentor does not hand you a map but teaches you to see the road. I am grateful that she saw something in a nervous girl with a broken lesson plan.
